title: What is `var` (local variable type inference, Java 10) — the compiler infers the type from the initializer so `var list = new ArrayList<String>()` is shorthand — where can it be used (local variables with an initializer, enhanced for-loop, try-with-resources), where can it NOT (fields, method parameters, return types, `var x = null`), and why is the variable still statically typed (it is NOT dynamic typing)?
shortTitle: What is the var keyword, where can and cannot it be used, and why is the variable still statically typed?

s1_definition.profdef: `var`, introduced in Java 10, is local variable type inference. It lets the compiler infer the static type of a local variable from the type of its initializer, so `var list = new ArrayList<String>()` is exactly equivalent to writing the full type `ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>()`. It is usable only for local variables with an initializer, for the loop variable in an enhanced for-loop, in a traditional for-loop, and in try-with-resources. It cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, catch parameters, or a local variable without an initializer, and it cannot infer from null. Crucially the variable remains STATICALLY typed; var is pure compile-time inference, not dynamic typing, so the type is fixed at compile time and cannot change.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh fills a form and, instead of writing the exact account type in a box, he lets the clerk read it off the document he is attaching and stamp the correct type automatically. That is var: the compiler looks at what you assign and stamps the precise type for you, saving you from writing a long type name twice. But the stamp is permanent and specific, decided the moment the form is filed. It is not a magic box that can later hold anything; if it was stamped as a savings-account reference, it stays a savings-account reference. The clerk also refuses to stamp if there is nothing attached to read from, which is why var needs an initializer and cannot be used with nothing or with null.
s1_definition.oneliner: var infers a local variable's type from its initializer at compile time, so it is shorthand for the full type and still fully statically typed, never dynamic.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `var`, introduced in Java 10, is local variable type inference. It lets the compiler infer the static type of a local variable from the type of its initializer, so `var list = new ArrayList<String>()` is exactly equivalent to writing the full type `ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<String>()`. It is usable only for local variables with an initializer, for the loop variable in an enhanced for-loop, in a traditional for-loop, and in try-with-resources. It cannot be used for fields, method parameters, return types, catch parameters, or a local variable without an initializer, and it cannot infer from null. Crucially the variable remains STATICALLY typed; var is pure compile-time inference, not dynamic typing, so the type is fixed at compile time and cannot change.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh fills a form and, instead of writing the exact account type in a box, he lets the clerk read it off the document he is attaching and stamp the correct type automatically. That is var: the compiler looks at what you assign and stamps the precise type for you, saving you from writing a long type name twice. But the stamp is permanent and specific, decided the moment the form is filed. It is not a magic box that can later hold anything; if it was stamped as a savings-account reference, it stays a savings-account reference. The clerk also refuses to stamp if there is nothing attached to read from, which is why var needs an initializer and cannot be used with nothing or with null.

**One line to remember:** var infers a local variable's type from its initializer at compile time, so it is shorthand for the full type and still fully statically typed, never dynamic.

sections.s2_technical:
var works by looking at the initializer on the right-hand side and inferring the variable's static type from it. So `var count = 10;` infers int, `var name = "Rajesh";` infers String, and `var balances = new ArrayList<BigDecimal>();` infers ArrayList of BigDecimal. The inferred type is exactly what the full declaration would have been, and the compiler substitutes it. This reduces verbose, repeated type names, especially for long generic types, and is most valuable when the right-hand side already makes the type obvious, such as a constructor call or a well-named factory method.

Where var is allowed: local variables inside a method with an initializer; the index or element variable of a for-loop, as in `for (var i = 0; i < n; i++)` and `for (var txn : transactions)`; and the resource variable in try-with-resources, as in `try (var reader = Files.newBufferedReader(path))`. In the for-each case, the element type is inferred from the collection's element type, so iterating a List of Account infers Account.

Where var is NOT allowed, and why. It cannot be used on fields of a class, because fields are part of the public type contract and must be explicit. It cannot be a method parameter or return type, again because those are part of the method's signature contract. It cannot be a catch parameter, because the exception type must be explicit. It cannot be a bare local declaration without an initializer, like `var x;`, because there is nothing to infer from. And it cannot infer from null, like `var x = null;`, because null has no specific type, so the compiler cannot choose one. There is also a subtlety with array initializers: `var arr = {1, 2, 3};` is illegal because the brace initializer has no standalone type, though `var arr = new int[]{1, 2, 3};` works.

The most important conceptual point is that var is NOT dynamic typing. Languages like Python or JavaScript let a variable hold any type and change type at runtime. var does nothing of the sort: the type is fixed at compile time from the initializer and is just as rigid as if you had written it out. So after `var s = "hello";`, assigning an int to s is a compile error exactly as it would be for a String variable. There is no runtime overhead, no reflection, and no loss of type checking; the generated bytecode is identical to writing the explicit type. This is why var is called local variable type inference, emphasizing inference and local.

Several style and gotcha points matter. var can infer surprising types, for example `var x = 1;` is int but `var y = 1L;` is long, and `var d = 0.1;` is double, so numeric literals still follow their own rules. With diamond syntax, `var list = new ArrayList<>();` infers ArrayList of Object, which is probably not intended, so you should write the type argument on the right. Inference can also pick a more specific type than you want, which can reduce flexibility, so for an interface-typed variable you may still prefer the explicit interface type, like `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();` rather than var, which would infer ArrayList. A senior engineer stresses using var where it improves readability by removing noisy duplication and the right-hand side is self-evident, and avoiding it where it hides the type and hurts comprehension, and reminds that there is a related `var` in lambda parameters since Java 11 but no connection to dynamic typing anywhere.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India refactored a verbose settlement method to use var for readability, and the exercise surfaced exactly where var helps and where it is illegal or misleading.

Problem 1 — the original code repeated long generic type names like a map of String to list of BigDecimal on both sides of an assignment, which was noisy, and var cleanly removes the duplication where the constructor already states the type. This is exactly the readability win of var for local variables with an obvious initializer.

Problem 2 — a developer tried to use var for a field, a method parameter, and a variable assigned null, and each failed to compile, which taught the team the precise boundaries of where var is allowed. This is exactly the set of disallowed positions.

Problem 3 — someone wrote var with a diamond on the right and got a list of Object instead of the intended element type, and someone else assumed var made a variable dynamic and tried to reassign an incompatible type, which failed. These demonstrate that var is static inference, not dynamic typing.

The fix uses var for local variables, the for-each loop, and try-with-resources where the type is evident, keeps explicit types for fields and signatures, writes the type argument on the right of the diamond, and shows a compile-error comment for the dynamic-typing misconception. The code defines an `Account`, a `SettlementService` with a `settle` method using var locals and a loop, and a `loadRates` method using try-with-resources. The demo settles transfers for Rajesh and Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts, Rajesh with a million and Priya with two hundred fifty thousand, and a list of two transfer amounts, forty-five thousand and twelve thousand.

Step 1. The demo declares Rajesh and Priya with var. The compiler reads the constructor call on the right and infers the static type Account for each, exactly as if Account had been written on the left. The variables are fully typed as Account.

Step 2. The transfers list is declared with var and initialized with List.of of two BigDecimals, so the compiler infers List of BigDecimal. This removes a repeated generic type name while keeping full type safety.

Step 3. The settle method uses var for a local total, which infers BigDecimal from BigDecimal.ZERO, and uses var in the for-each loop, where the element type is inferred as BigDecimal from the list's element type. Each iteration debits the from account, credits the to account, and adds to the total.

Step 4. After processing both transfers, Rajesh's balance is reduced by the total fifty-seven thousand and Priya's is increased by the same, and the method returns the total as a BigDecimal. The return type is explicit because var is not allowed on return types.

Step 5. The comments show the key boundaries: reassigning an int to a var-inferred String fails to compile, proving var is static not dynamic; and var on a field, a parameter, a return type, or with null is illegal. The HashMap in loadRates writes the type arguments on the right of the diamond so var infers HashMap of String to BigDecimal rather than of Object.

Step 6. The demo logs the settled total and the updated balances, confirming that var produced identical behavior to explicit types while improving readability for the obvious locals.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 19:11:40 [INFO] settled total = 57000.00, Rajesh=943000.00, Priya=307000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Inference at compile time (NOT runtime) ──
  var rajesh = new Account(...)        → inferred type: Account
  var transfers = List.of(bd1, bd2)    → inferred type: List<BigDecimal>
  var total = BigDecimal.ZERO          → inferred type: BigDecimal
  for (var amount : transfers)         → inferred type: BigDecimal

       │ compiler substitutes the exact type; bytecode identical to explicit
       ▼
  settle(from, to, transfers)
    total = ZERO
    ├─ amount 45000 → from.debit, to.credit, total=45000
    └─ amount 12000 → from.debit, to.credit, total=57000
       ▼
  return 57000.00 ; Rajesh 943000.00 ; Priya 307000.00

  ── Illegal / misconception (compile errors) ──
  var x;              ✗ no initializer
  var x = null;       ✗ cannot infer from null
  field/param/return  ✗ var not allowed (signature contract)
  var s="hi"; s=42;   ✗ STILL static — int not assignable to String
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
var, introduced in Java 10, is local variable type inference. It lets the compiler infer the static type of a local variable from the type of its initializer, so declaring a variable as var equal to a new ArrayList of String is exactly equivalent to writing the full type on the left. It reduces noisy, repeated type names, and it is most valuable when the right-hand side already makes the type obvious, such as a constructor call or a well-named factory method.

var is allowed for local variables with an initializer, for the index or element variable of a for-loop, for the element in a for-each loop where the type is inferred from the collection, and for the resource variable in try-with-resources. It is not allowed for fields, method parameters, return types, or catch parameters, because those are part of a type contract that must be explicit, and it is not allowed for a local declaration without an initializer or with null, because there is nothing with a definite type to infer from.

The most important point I always stress is that var is not dynamic typing. The type is fixed at compile time from the initializer and is just as rigid as if I had written it out, so after inferring String I cannot later assign an int, it is a compile error. There is no runtime overhead, no reflection, and no loss of type checking, and the generated bytecode is identical to using the explicit type. That is why it is called local variable type inference, emphasizing inference and local, not dynamic.

In our settlement service at National Bank of India, I refactored a verbose method that repeated long generic type names on both sides of assignments, and var cleanly removed the duplication for locals where the constructor already stated the type, while I kept explicit types on the fields and the method signatures because those are contracts. The exercise also taught the team the boundaries: var on a field, a parameter, or a null failed to compile, a diamond on the right of var inferred a list of Object until we wrote the type argument on the right, and a developer who assumed var made a variable dynamic found that reassigning an incompatible type was a compile error. My guidance is to use var where it improves readability and the type is self-evident, and to keep the explicit type where it aids comprehension or where the language requires it.
